opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the central challenge is that the natural world doesn't come to us in the neat, discrete form that language or images do. When you look at fluid flows, weather, materials, or molecules, you're dealing with continuous phenomena that span many scales, from the atomic level all the way up to the planetary level. A lot of the AI tools we've built so far, especially large language models, are great at pattern-matching over tokens, but they aren't built to understand physics. They can describe what a hurricane is, but they can't simulate one accurately.

So the question becomes: how do we build AI that actually captures the underlying physical laws and can generalize beyond the data it was trained on? That's what led us to work on neural operators. The idea is to learn mappings between function spaces, not just between fixed-size vectors. This lets the model work at any resolution, and lets you train on coarse data and still query at fine resolution. That matters enormously in science, because the phenomena you care about often happen at scales you can't afford to simulate everywhere with traditional numerical solvers.

The other piece is data. In science, data is often scarce, expensive, or noisy, but we have centuries of accumulated knowledge in the form of equations and physical constraints. So the challenge, and the opportunity, is combining the two: using data where we have it, and physics where we know it, so the models remain trustworthy and consistent. We've seen this pay off in weather forecasting with models like FourCastNet, which are tens of thousands of times faster than traditional numerical weather prediction while staying competitive in accuracy.

Ultimately, I think the goal isn't just to speed up existing simulations. It's to get to a place where AI becomes a genuine partner in discovery, helping us design new materials, new drugs, and better engineering systems, and closing the loop between simulation, experiment, and design in a way that just wasn't possible before.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical simulation and discovery, but does not identify real-world hypothesis testing and verification as the bottleneck relative to idea generation.

r002.rationale: It says AI should capture physical laws and combine data with equations and physical constraints so models remain trustworthy and consistent in scientific domains.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose combining language models with formal verification to check mathematical claims.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that science and AI have very different definitions of success, and the central challenge is bridging that gap.

In the machine learning world, we got very comfortable with a certain recipe: collect a huge dataset, train a big model on it, and measure yourself on a benchmark. That works beautifully for language and images because the data is essentially free and the evaluation is "does a human think this looks right." Science doesn't work like that. In science, the ground truth is physics. It's the laws of nature, and those laws don't care whether your output looks plausible. If you're simulating a fluid or predicting the weather or designing a catheter or a drug molecule, being approximately right in a way that violates conservation of mass or energy is not useful. It can actually be dangerous.

So the first piece of the challenge is that data is expensive and scarce. You don't have trillions of tokens of turbulence. Every data point might come from a wind tunnel experiment or a supercomputer run that costs thousands of GPU hours. That forces you to be much more thoughtful about what you're learning. This is why I've spent so much time on neural operators. Instead of learning a mapping between fixed-size arrays, you learn the mapping between functions, between continuous fields. That lets you train at one resolution and query at another, which is something a standard neural network simply can't do, and it's closer to how a physicist actually thinks about the problem.

The second piece is that you have to put the physics back in. Pure data-driven models extrapolate badly, and science is all about extrapolation. We want to go to regimes we've never observed, new materials, new climates, new pressures. So the question becomes how you encode symmetries, constraints, and known equations into the model, not as a nice-to-have but as a structural part of the learning. When you do that, you can get speedups of tens of thousands of times over traditional numerical solvers while still respecting the underlying physics. That's what turns AI from a curiosity into something an engineer can actually use in a design loop.

And the third piece, which people underestimate, is cultural. Scientists and ML researchers literally speak different languages. A domain scientist will say "my simulation takes two weeks," and an ML person will hear "I need more data." Getting these groups into the same room, working on the same problem with shared vocabulary, is honestly as hard as any technical problem. The projects that have worked best for me have always been the ones where a domain expert was a true co-owner from day one, not someone handing over a dataset at the end.

So if I had to compress it into one sentence: the challenge is that AI learned to imitate, and science requires you to understand. Closing that gap, making models that generalize because they capture structure rather than because they've memorized, is what the next decade is really about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scarce scientific data and the need to respect physical laws, but does not identify real-world hypothesis testing and verification as the bottleneck or contrast it with generating ideas.

r002.rationale: It says physics, constraints, and known equations should be built into models so they respect underlying physics and can be used in engineering design.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose combining language models with formal verification to check mathematical claims.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is bringing together learning from data and the scientific knowledge we already have. In science, we’re rarely starting from a blank slate. We have physical laws, mathematical models, and simulations. The question is how to build AI that can use that structure while learning what our existing models don’t capture.

And the standard for success has to go beyond fitting the data we’ve seen. Can the model predict what happens under new conditions? Can we understand when it’s unreliable? Can it help us design an experiment that teaches us something new? That’s where the connection becomes really powerful: when AI becomes part of the process of scientific discovery.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prediction under new conditions and designing informative experiments, but does not identify real-world hypothesis testing and verification as the bottleneck relative to idea generation.

r002.rationale: It says AI should use physical laws and other scientific structure, but does not clearly present preserving correct physics in models as the way to ensure they work in physical domains.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention language models or formal verification of mathematical claims.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is bringing together learning from data with the structure we already know about the physical world. In science, we have physical laws, symmetries, and conservation principles. How do we build those into AI so that it can learn efficiently and make predictions that remain physically meaningful?

And scientific discovery requires more than a prediction that looks plausible. We need to understand where a model is reliable, quantify its uncertainty, and validate it through simulations and experiments. That creates a powerful loop: AI helps us explore possibilities, experiments test them, and those results improve the model.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments test possibilities and improve the model, but does not identify real-world testing and verification as the bottleneck or contrast it with generating ideas.

r002.rationale: It presents incorporating physical laws and principles into AI as a way to make its predictions physically meaningful.
